utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, as far as this item is concerned, Your Honour, I think there is a matter that we need to address in the absence of the witness. I apologise, but it's something of serious importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's in addition to what was submitted by Ms. Vidovic two days ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, we need to draw down the curtains. Sorry about this, Ms. Sellers, but obviously we need to address this matter, whatever it is. Sir, you need to leave the courtroom for a short while while we receive submissions from the Defence on this document. And then after that, you'll come back and we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you may proceed straight away, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's two matters really in relation to this. The first is that, as Your Honour will recall, on a -- on at least one occasion, and I don't have the reference with me but I can find it, my colleague was stopped from putting to a witness what someone else had said, and the ruling was that that's not proper, that one can ask if someone was to say such-and-such, what would your response be. There are good reasons for that rule. That's one aspect. The second aspect is of course if we're talking about statements going into evidence for some purpose other than, for example, prior inconsistent statements, which we discussed the other day, which are being used to impeach the witness, then there are the provisions of Rule 92 bis, et cetera. It's a carefully regulated area because of course if we're not careful, the Prosecution will later seek to rely on this as a statement introduced in evidence, in this case totally bypassing 92 bis and invite Your Honours to treat this as evidence, and before we know it, through the back door and avoiding 92 bis, the Prosecution could introduce a hundred statements of people we haven't cross-examined, who we didn't have any opportunity to object to their statement. And there were statements in evidence which the Prosecution is going to rely on. That has to be wholly wrong. It has to be wrong. And it is Rule 92 bis, as I say, which regulates that. And so I wonder why the Prosecution is seeking to put this statement - alleged statement, I should say - before the witness when Ms. Sellers can quite simply say, If I were to say such-and-such, or do you know so-and-so and simply put the propositions to the witness. But I'm very worried that there's going to be an attempt through the back door to get statements in, and then at the end of the trial Your Honours will be invited to treat this as evidence and we will have been wholly deprived of any opportunity to challenge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. With regard to this last point, obviously I don't need to repeat what I have already stated on several occasions involving, if not identical, similar issues that this could never, according to procedural law, be considered as evidence, under no circumstances, and please do remember that we are three professional Judges here with a lot of experience behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's a helpful indication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It didn't even cross our minds to consider this if admitted in evidence as evidence of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would remain an unsworn statement by someone who has not been made available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I please address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Rajko Jovanovic was not a witness of the Prosecution, was he?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he was not. Might I address on the points raised by Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have the points. Why do you want to put this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Jones has raised some very interesting points and among which is statements that come from people since the Defence has used, and I go back to D135, a statement -- a prior statement from one of our witnesses and that they have claimed that they've only used this to show prior inconsistencies where I think that we can certainly find on the record that D135 has been used to corroborate evidence of their witnesses. We remember the discussion of Zuti, whether it's blond or not, which was found in a statement of a witness when he gave something of this nature. You can remember that they've used that statement in order to corroborate whether there was a facility in Fakovici that would be triggered and then burned. And now to stand up and say that with a statement that is essentially of the same nature that we should be limited to only prior inconsistent statements, I believe is fundamentally inconsistent. But turning to, I think, more significant arguments. Mr. Jones has already anticipated what the use of this statement is as opposed to maybe considering that there's material in here that appears to support some of the testimony of the witness that they have brought forward, and he can always be asked his opinion in terms of factual knowledge of what appears in the statement. Now, the Defence in their direct examination led evidence as to what was a military presence in Jezestica. We have laid a foundation with that. The witness agrees that there was an attack that day. I think this statement might be corroborative of his testimony at this point, not necessarily inconsistent. And in order to try and pre-empt Your Honours from looking at this piece of evidence in whatever manner you may choose to look at it and choose to weigh it was trying to get assurance that it will not seem to be credible, I think it is in one way counter to any of the introduction of documents or pieces of evidence. Your Honours, I leave this in your hands after you see our use of the statement to decide on whether it should enter into evidence and the proper weight that's attributed to it. And I hope that similar to D135 we will view this in the appropriate manner in which it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers, before I give the floor to Mr. Jones. But do you mean to say that basically you're going to confront the witness with some of the facts that are contained in this statement? And if he answers no, then you are going to juxtapose the contents of or contrast the contents of this statement to his testimony? Because if that is the case, Mr. Jones is 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I intended to do was to show how parts of this statement are consistent with things that this witness has testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. Why bring forward a statement by a person who is not being made available for cross-examination? It's having one witness who is testifying under oath here who is making affirmations of this and of that being confronted with a statement of an un -- as far as I am concerned, an unknown person who is not available. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Put to the questions -- put to the witness the various facts as they result from this document that you wish him to testify upon, see what his answers are, and then ask yourself whether it would be regular procedurally then to present this document in evidence by way of either contradicting what he is saying or confirming what he is saying. By confirming what he is saying, I don't think you need it. And contradicting the witness, you wouldn't -- you wouldn't do it in this way. You would do it in some other way, but not by bringing forward a document which cannot be contested by the other side because the person who allegedly made this statement is not available. I mean, I have never come across a procedural -- a procedure like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we have in this trial at times had -- in particular, the Defence put books before witnesses. We are not questioning the authors of the books, bringing the authors of the books in to find out where did passages come from, where did statements come from, but yet we allow a witness's testimony to either be corroborated, contradicted, confirmed, and repeatedly ask them for passages: Is this correct? Does this reflect not? Not to belabour the point, Your Honour, but I wanted to emphasise that this is corroborative and this is not to impeach, and this goes -- this evidence goes just a bit further than what he has said on a couple of incidents. I think the real fear of the Defence doesn't lie in the inability to cross-examine this witness but just what this document might plainly say on its face.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then precisely. You want to admit this document in evidence in substitution of what the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- person, Rajko Jovanovic, could state under oath here if he was made available.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does not seek to enter it for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do feel bound to reply, because Ms. Sellers' answer was disingenuous in the extreme on a number of accounts. Firstly, in terms of this prior inconsistent statement, D135, I think it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget that. We are not discussing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I simply wish to make the point that when we mention Zuti and a yellow gun, it's to -- again, it's to impeach the witness because he denied shooting from the gun, and any question we ever designed -- which we asked was designed to show that he had not given truthful testimony here. The problem --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, they used it with their own witness. If we have to make sure that these arguments --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may not be interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish, Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is really discourteous. Your Honour, going back to the fundamentals of the procedure adopted here, let's say we had a witness and I say, Well, Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic said such-and-such, what do you say about that? Or Pyers Tucker said such-and-such. Obviously that's -- that's not permissible, otherwise we'll spend the whole trial putting bits of people's testimony to new witnesses. So what firstly I ask is the difference between that and having a document. Let's say we printed off the transcript document, we passed it to them, This is what Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic said, what do you say about that. The principle is the same in each case, that you shouldn't be asking a witness to comment on what someone else has said. It seems to be that the Prosecution thinks because this is a document then that changes everything. In any event, the fundamental point which I -- which I would submit, Your Honours, is the following: That Ms. Sellers is saying that the purpose of introducing this document is not to impeach this witness but to corroborate what he's saying, as if the Prosecution wishes to bolster the credibility of one of our witnesses. That's obviously not what they're saying, and that's obviously why it's disingenuous because in fact what they want to do is have this witness confirm certain parts of this alleged statement, then introduce into evidence and then say, Oh, look, this witness says that they burnt everything down. That helps support our allegations that the Muslims destroyed houses in Jezestica. That's what they're trying to do, and that's completely improper. Let me give an example of what might be a simple situation. Let's say Your Honours reject our 92 bis motion for Donald Paris and another witness comes along and I give Donald Paris's statement and I put it in front of him, and I say, Was there starvation in Srebrenica; yes, there was. Oh, exhibit number, please, and then we've got an exhibit. And then I will rely on Donald Paris's statement as evidence of all the other matters. That indicates how the Prosecution can simply get around calling witnesses by introducing statements in this way. I would say finally, Your Honour, that Your Honours have made it crystal clear to us that you're not going to treat statements such as these, alleged statements, as being evidence of the truth of its contents. Ms. Sellers - and I can find the reference, but I don't want to delay matters - says that we're trying to pre-empt the issue and Your Honours should be able to give whatever weight you like to it. So in fact they're not accepting your ruling on this. They're going to invite you at the end of the trial to take this as evidence of the truth of its contents. It's clear the Prosecution is not excluding that. And that's why I'm so concerned, and that's why of course we needed to mention the issue now. Because we know full well in their post-trial brief the Prosecution are going to say: Here is further evidence of the crimes in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just please reply on one factual misrepresentation by the Defence. Unless it was genuous [sic] misunderstanding, when I'm referring to the use of D135, I'm not referring to their use of it as a statement that contradicted the Prosecution witness. I'm referring to their repeated use of it to corroborate the testimony of Defence witnesses. If I can just clear that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was never used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are going out for a couple of minutes, and we'll come back with our decision. --- Break taken at 1.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, our decision is as follows, Ms. Sellers and Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic, Mr. Wubben: That of course you can -- you're free to make use of any part of this statement with this witness by putting to him the facts that appear here and asking him -- asking for his reaction. However, you are not entitled to put to him the fact that these are stated by anyone in particular, particularly by Rajko Jovanovic. And that being so, we don't see a point in then moving forward to try and contradict any of the statements of the witness by filing this statement as a document, because as it is it can never become evidence or substitute what would be the evidence of Mr. Rajko Jovanovic if he were to be produced here. So that's our position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just have that clarified, meaning that I can use any part of the statement in terms of putting questions forward?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. But you cannot tell him: My name is Rajko Jovanovic, son of Milovan, born -- when I say any part of the statement, any part that can reasonably be made use of in conformity with the ruling that we have just given.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it seems that -- I cannot see the prior transcript, but I think in describing the document I've already stated it was a statement from Rajko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. But anyway, I can remedy that because I can tell the witness: Forget what has been stated beforehand. We are moving to something different, and you will be asked questions on something else. Yes, and I don't think we even ought to have this in our possession. The witness had a copy of it already? He saw it already? Yeah, okay. But he didn't have time to read it because he was -- anyway, there is no other remedy that I can think of at the present moment, Mr. Jones and Ms. Sellers. I will just pretend and hopefully I am still good at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stand in your hands. If you would like to ask the witness not to refer to it or look at it, I am perfectly fine with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But in the meantime, I will just check what happened before. All right. You had said: "Sir, I want to draw your attention to a couple of things" -- yes, you have already mentioned this. All right. I will see how I can remedy this, and if you don't like what I do, then please stand up and say so. It won't be the first and it won't be the last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, we have discussed what we needed to discuss and we have taken a decision. Fortunately for you, you don't have to bother any further with that document that was given to you before and the gentleman who supposedly made that statement. We will be moving to something else, something different, however which still relates to the attack on Jezestica of the 8th of August. So basically, you will be asked on the same event but not in relation to that piece of paper that you were given before. So, Ms. Sellers, and we only have about five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm quite aware, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, you testified earlier that during World War II that there had been crimes committed against Bosnian Muslims by Bosnian Serbs who lived or still lived in your region. Do you remember your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you agree that there might have been some Bosnian Serbs who felt that during that same period crimes had been committed against them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your prior testimony seemed to have indicated that people who commit crimes, particularly during war, should be tried and punished. Would you agree with me that, if I understand correctly, that's how you would have expressed yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What war? Could you tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm talking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, firstly we have gone back to another war. I don't see the relevance of the Second World War to this trial. Secondly, I think this is the second occasion where Ms. Sellers is seeking from a lay witness his expert opinion as to whether people should be tried for crimes. And, again, I don't think it's something which this Chamber needs a witness to tell them whether or not a crime should be punished. I don't see where Ms. Sellers is going with this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unfortunately you were not here when this witness started his testimony on Monday or Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I read the transcripts fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he dealt with the crimes committed during the Second World War, particularly by two persons, Ejub and I forgot --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, who feature in this war. It was directly relevant to people in Kravica in 1992, to their activities, to specific events in Kravica. It wasn't a wide-ranging inquest into who was responsible for crimes in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If Your Honours might please, if in my last 30 seconds I can state that I'm certainly referring to World War II. I think I've indicated that I'm going back to the same geographical period that sir has indicated when discussing crimes from World War II and, as a matter of fact, discussing those crimes committed against, among, between the same group. I'm certain that that was my 15 seconds, and so I would just say that I believe that I'm well within the scope of cross-examination as to what was led on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, and if you don't think you will finish on this in two minutes or three minutes, then we'll adjourn and continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not finish on this, and it's unfortunate because I would have liked to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, but I think -- I'm stopping you here. It's wiser to stop here than to proceed and then have to stop in any case halfway. So we will continue on Monday morning at 9.00. I think it's still in this courtroom. Yeah. I think it's Courtroom I. 9.00 on Monday, and hopefully we'll finish with you on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of November, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
